client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away last year in that car accident. Everything just feels kind of gray and flat now — things I used to enjoy don't really do anything for me anymore. I've also been pulling away from my friends, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: What you're carrying — the loss of your brother, the grayness, the pulling away — that's an enormous weight, and I'm really glad you're here even if part of you isn't sure it will help. I notice that as you're describing all of this, your words sound almost matter-of-fact, but I wonder if underneath that there's something much heavier that hasn't quite had space to come out yet. What does it feel like in your body right now, as you talk about him?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, there's this kind of tightness in my chest, like something's just sitting there and won't move. And my throat feels a little constricted right now, which is annoying because I really didn't want to get emotional about this today. I guess I've been keeping it pretty contained because if I start actually feeling it, I don't know what happens next.
therapist: That tightness and constriction you're feeling right now — that's actually the grief asking to be noticed, and it makes so much sense that you've been holding it at arm's length when "what happens next" feels unknown and scary. There's a lot of courage in what you just said, because that fear of losing control if you let yourself feel it is one of the heaviest parts of grief. I'm curious — when you imagine actually letting that tightness move, what's the worst thing you think might happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the worst thing is that I'd just completely fall apart and not be able to put myself back together again. Like, I've been functional — going to work, doing the basic stuff — and if I let it out, I'm scared I'd lose even that. And then I'd really be alone, because I've already pushed most people away and there'd be no one there to help pick up the pieces.
therapist: That fear of falling apart and having no one there to catch you — that's such a painful place to be, and it makes complete sense that "staying functional" has felt like the only safe option. What I want to gently offer is that the falling apart you're afraid of and the kind of grief that actually moves through you are often very different things — people are usually more resilient than that fear suggests. And I'm also noticing that the isolation you're describing, the pushing people away, might actually be making that fear feel even bigger than it really is — what do you think would happen if you let even one person back in, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but it's not that simple, because the people I've pulled away from — they didn't really know how to handle it either. A couple of them said really clumsy things right after he died, like trying to find silver linings, and it just made me feel more alone than if they'd said nothing. So now there's this wall there, and I don't even know if letting someone in would help or just remind me how much people don't get it.
therapist: That experience of reaching out — or being reached out to — and coming away feeling *more* alone is one of the most isolating things grief can do, and it makes complete sense that it built a wall. Those clumsy silver-lining comments, even when well-meaning, can feel like people are trying to take your pain away rather than just sit with you in it. I'm wondering — has there ever been even one moment with someone, maybe even briefly, where you felt even a little bit understood in this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: There was actually one moment, maybe a month after the accident, where my coworker just sat with me in the break room and didn't say anything for a while. She'd lost her mom a few years back, and she just said "this is really awful and there's nothing that makes it okay," and something about that cracked me open a little in a way that felt almost like relief. But I haven't really talked to her since then, and I guess I convinced myself it was a one-time thing, that she was just being polite.
therapist: That moment with your coworker sounds like exactly the kind of being-seen that grief needs — no fixing, no silver linings, just someone saying "this is awful" and meaning it. And I notice that even as you describe it as a relief, there's something in how you're telling me about it that sounds a little raw, like it still means a lot more to you than "just polite." What do you think it would take to reach out to her again — not to have a big conversation, but just to let her know that moment mattered to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think part of me wants to, but then I start worrying that I'll make it weird, or that she's moved on and doesn't think about it the way I do. There's also this guilt that's crept in because I basically disappeared on her after that, and reaching out now feels like I'd have to explain that or apologize for it. I don't know if I'm ready to open that door when I can barely hold it together as it is.
therapist: The guilt about disappearing, the worry about making it weird — those are such common ways our minds try to protect us from the vulnerability of reconnecting, but they can also keep us stuck in the very isolation that's hurting us. Here's something worth considering: she lost her mom, she sat with you in silence, she said "there's nothing that makes it okay" — she already speaks the language of grief, and someone like that is unlikely to need a formal explanation or apology. What if reaching out didn't have to be a big door-opening, but just a small crack — even a simple message saying her kindness stayed with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when you put it that way, it sounds less terrifying than what I'd built it up to be in my head. But I still feel this knot in my stomach about it, like even a small message opens me up to something I can't predict or control. What if she responds warmly and then I actually have to follow through with being less alone — that almost scares me as much as her not responding at all.
therapist: What you just named is really profound — that being welcomed back into connection is just as frightening as being rejected, because it would mean actually having to let yourself be less alone. That fear makes a lot of sense when grief has taught you that closeness can also mean more to lose. I'm curious — when you imagine her responding warmly and you actually following through, what is it specifically that feels so unsafe about being cared for right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it's because if I let someone care for me, it makes the loss feel more real somehow — like right now I can keep it at a certain distance by staying numb and isolated, but warmth and connection would crack that open. And there's also this guilt underneath it all, like I don't deserve to feel better or be comforted when my brother is just gone and that's never changing. It's almost like staying in the gray feels like the only way I can still be loyal to him.
therapist: What you just said — that staying in the gray feels like loyalty to your brother — is one of the most honest and heartbreaking things you could have named, and I want to sit with that for a moment. Grief can quietly convince us that healing is a kind of betrayal, but I wonder what your brother would actually want for you if he could see you right now. Do you think he would recognize staying numb and alone as the way you honor him, or might he want something different for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question really gets to me, because honestly, no — he would have hated seeing me like this. He was always the one pushing me to get out, call people back, not take life so seriously, and I can almost hear him giving me a hard time about hiding away. But knowing that doesn't automatically make the guilt go away, because there's still this voice that says feeling better means moving on, and moving on means leaving him behind.
therapist: The way you just described him — pushing you to get out, not take life so seriously, giving you a hard time — there's so much love in that, and it sounds like you can still hear him so clearly. What I want to gently offer is that moving on and leaving him behind are not the same thing; carrying him forward into a life he would have wanted for you might actually be the truest way to keep him close. What do you think it would look like to honor who he was by letting a little of that warmth he pushed you toward back in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe actually lands differently than I expected, because you're right that he was always about connection and not shutting yourself off. I think honoring him might look something like sending that message to my coworker, not because I'm ready to be okay, but because he would have already sent it three weeks ago and rolled his eyes at me for waiting this long. It still feels scary, but framing it as something he would have pushed me to do makes it feel a little less like betrayal and a little more like... him still being here in some way.
therapist: That image of him rolling his eyes at you for waiting this long — I can feel how alive he still is in you when you talk about him like that, and there's something really beautiful and painful happening all at once right now. Your words are finding something hopeful, and I also notice there's a lot of energy and emotion coming through as you say it, like this reframe is touching something deep that's still very raw. Be gentle with yourself as you sit with this — what feels like the very first small step you could take today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
